sections.text: WS-POL-J – Students with Disabilities and Human Decision Safeguards Analysis

The strongest overall conclusion is that WS-POL-J is one of the committee’s strongest human-safeguard sections. The record shows broad agreement that IEP/504 and other required determinations must remain human-led, that AI may be assistive at most, and that uses affecting students with disabilities require stronger review for accessibility, bias, documentation, and accountability. The main disagreements are narrower: how much assistive AI use to permit, whether informed consent or advance disclosure should be required for some uses, and how explicit the policy should be about accommodations, accessibility review, and ongoing disparate-impact monitoring.

heading_path: Core conclusion
sections.text: The public record supports four high-confidence conclusions.

heading_path: Core conclusion
sections.text: First, the committee’s center of gravity is clearly that eligibility, placement, discipline-linked determinations, and other legally consequential decisions cannot be delegated to AI. That principle appears in the V3 outline as Decision 7, where discipline, IEP/504, and other required determinations remain human-led; AI may assist but not substitute; and any use must be documented, supervised, and constrained.

heading_path: Core conclusion
sections.text: Second, the committee appears to agree that AI uses affecting students with disabilities should be reviewed not only for privacy and bias, but also for accessibility and accommodation conflict. The Equity & Access deliverable explicitly asks whether a use conflicts with accommodations or assistive technology, adds barriers for sensory/attention/motor needs, or creates inequity for multilingual learners. (D-EQA-1)

heading_path: Core conclusion
sections.text: Third, the record supports a strong expectation that tools affecting protected groups or consequential educational outcomes require stronger governance review, not ordinary classroom discretion alone. The D-DPS workstream does this through tiered review and special handling for consequential uses and sensitive records.

heading_path: Core conclusion
sections.text: Fourth, the record shows less disagreement about the human-led principle itself than about the boundary between assistive use and impermissible substitution.

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: This section grows out of the committee’s broader move from general values to guardrails for consequential decisions. By the time the V3 outline was posted, the committee had already separated:

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: staff and teacher use,

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: student use,

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: privacy and procurement governance,

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text:
and, in WS-POL-J, students with disabilities and human decision safeguards.
That placement matters. It suggests the committee understood disability-related AI use as more than a subtopic of equity or privacy. It is a distinct policy area requiring explicit safeguards.

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: The Meeting 4 readiness snapshot reinforces that reading. It shows D-EQA-1 and D-DPS-1 as active deliverables informing the recommendation outline, while D-CCI-1 and D-IPC-1 were still not started in the public snapshot. For WS-POL-J, that means the strongest documentary base comes from equity/access, privacy/security/governance, the outline, and the survey, rather than from communications or implementation planning. (Meeting 4 readiness)

1. Human-led decisions are the baseline
sections.text: The clearest shared ground is the human-led rule. The V3 outline says:

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
1. Human-led decisions are the baseline
sections.text: The survey supports that strongly. The prompt “IEP/504 decisions stay human” was widely approved or only lightly revised. Even many respondents with different overall postures accepted the core principle that eligibility, placement, or required determinations should not be delegated to AI. (Survey export)

2. Accessibility and accommodation conflict must be reviewed explicitly
sections.text: The strongest workstream evidence here comes from D-EQA-1. Its rapid triage asks whether a proposed use:

or creates inequity for students developing English.
Its deep-dive prompts then ask which accommodations apply, how a tool might undermine approved supports, and what guidance or professional development is required for consistent implementation. (D-EQA-1)

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
2. Accessibility and accommodation conflict must be reviewed explicitly
sections.text: That is a strong sign that the committee did not view “students with disabilities” mainly through a legal-compliance lens alone. It also viewed the issue as one of practical instructional fit and assistive-technology compatibility.

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
3. Consequential uses require stronger governance
sections.text: The D-DPS draft aligns closely with WS-POL-J even though it is a privacy/governance workstream. It treats consequential uses, identity-linked uses, and sensitive records as escalated cases requiring stronger review, and it crosswalks those decisions to FERPA, IDEA, Section 504/ADA, COPPA, and vendor/data-protection requirements. That means the committee was not relying only on educator judgment for these contexts. It was building a governance layer around them.

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
4. Bias and disparate-impact monitoring are part of the safeguard model
sections.text: The V3 outline explicitly calls for tools affecting protected groups to receive pre-adoption bias and accessibility review and ongoing monitoring for disparate impact. D-EQA-1 operationalizes that through its risk ratings, mitigation actions, and equity metrics, including subgroup disaggregation and tracking conflicts with IEP/504 supports. (D-EQA-1)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: This is the biggest substantive split.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: The outline position is moderate: AI may assist but not substitute; uses must be supervised, documented, and constrained. That leaves room for some assistive functions.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: Several survey responses support that middle position. One respondent approved language that AI may support documentation or analysis, but not required determinations. Another proposed wording such as: FCCPS will not delegate student assessments or decisions as to eligibility, placement, or progress to AI; any AI use must be assistive, supervised, and documented. That is a classic guardrailed-assistance posture. (Survey export)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: A stricter position is also visible. One respondent proposed that FCCPS may not use any generative AI to assist with the composition of documents bearing on discipline or disability accommodations unless use is previously disclosed and informed consent is provided by all affected parties. Another objected that earlier human-written language had been softened into “AI is fine to use, just document it,” and tried to restore a more restrictive anti-AI intent around IEPs and related determinations. That is not a total rejection of all AI, but it is much closer to a consent-first / use-minimization posture. (Survey export)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: 2. Documentation and disclosure vs. informed consent

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: The committee seems broadly comfortable with documentation. The outline itself requires that AI use in these contexts be documented, supervised, and constrained.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: But there is meaningful disagreement over whether documentation is enough. Some respondents appear satisfied with documentation plus human leadership. Others argue that where disability accommodations, medical-style notes, discipline, or eligibility are involved, the district should go further and require informed consent from affected parties before using AI assistance at all.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: This is a genuine philosophical difference:

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: one side sees documentation and governance as sufficient safeguards,

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Assistive use allowed under supervision vs. much narrower use
sections.text: the other sees these contexts as sensitive enough to require something closer to affirmative permission.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
3. Policy-level rule vs. implementation-level mechanism
sections.text: The public record suggests fairly strong agreement on the principle, but less clarity on the operational mechanics.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
3. Policy-level rule vs. implementation-level mechanism
sections.text: The V3 outline states the policy-level rule clearly. D-EQA-1 then asks whether mitigations should live in policy, guidance, PD, or tool governance. D-DPS similarly crosswalks decisions into procurement, approval, legal review, and retention rules. This suggests the committee may agree on the “human-led” standard while still differing on how much of the implementation detail should appear directly in policy text versus in procedures and checklists. (D-EQA-1)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Disability-specific safeguards vs. broader protected-groups framing
sections.text: The outline frames this section partly through students with disabilities and partly through tools affecting protected groups. That is important. It suggests some members may prefer a narrower disability/IEP/504 focus, while others favor a broader civil-rights lens that includes disability, language, and other protected-group risks.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Disability-specific safeguards vs. broader protected-groups framing
sections.text: D-EQA-1 strongly supports the broader lens by pairing disability/accommodation review with ELL, access, bias, and enforcement-fairness questions. That may make the section more powerful, but it can also broaden it beyond what some members think WS-POL-J should cover.

heading_path: Best characterization of the range of opinions
sections.text: The accessible record suggests three main positions.

heading_path: Best characterization of the range of opinions
sections.text: A guardrailed human-led position appears to be the committee center: IEP/504 and similar determinations remain human-led; AI may assist in limited ways; all such use must be supervised, documented, and constrained; accessibility and bias review are required.

heading_path: Best characterization of the range of opinions
sections.text: A stricter consent-first position accepts the human-led principle but is much less comfortable with any AI use touching disability accommodations, discipline, or eligibility, and may require prior disclosure and informed consent.

heading_path: Best characterization of the range of opinions
sections.text: A governance-heavy implementation position emphasizes that the principle is not enough by itself; approval tiers, legal crosswalks, procurement controls, documentation, accessibility testing, and equity monitoring are necessary to make the safeguard real. This is the posture most visible in D-DPS and D-EQA. (D-EQA-1)

sections.text: For WS-POL-J, the strongest committee-grounded common ground is:
